name: Scalability
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Blockchain Trilemma: Why You Can't Just Make the Blocks Bigger
lesson.summary: Scalability is a blockchain's ability to handle growing transaction demand without giving up decentralization or security, and the tension among these three goals, often called the blockchain trilemma, explains why raising throughput is never as simple as it sounds.
lesson.body:
A blockchain, as defined earlier, is a ledger replicated across many independent nodes, where each node independently verifies every recorded transaction rather than trusting a central authority to do so. That replication is exactly what makes the ledger trustworthy without a middleman, and it is also exactly what makes scaling a blockchain a fundamentally different problem than scaling an ordinary centralized database. A company that needs more database capacity can simply add more servers under its own control. A blockchain cannot casually do the equivalent, because every additional unit of transaction throughput has to be independently processed and stored by a broad, decentralized set of node operators, not just by whichever party wants the extra capacity.

This tension is often summarized as the blockchain trilemma, a framing popularized by Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin, which holds that decentralization, security, and scalability are difficult to maximize all at once. Decentralization means a large, diverse set of independent participants can run and verify the network. Security means the network resists attempts to rewrite or corrupt its history. Scalability means the network can process a high volume of transactions. Pushing hard on any one of these tends to strain at least one of the other two.

The connection to transaction throughput and network latency, both covered earlier, makes this concrete. Raising throughput by increasing block size or shortening block time increases the volume of data every node must download, verify, and store in a given period. Because blocks must physically propagate across a globally distributed network before the next block can safely build on them, larger or more frequent blocks take longer, relative to the block interval, to reach every node. Slower or less well resourced node operators fall further behind, and participation tends to concentrate among those with the fastest connections and most powerful hardware, which is a loss of decentralization. Bitcoin's contentious block size debate of 2015 through 2017, which ultimately led a dissenting faction to fork off the separate Bitcoin Cash network specifically to raise the block size limit, was essentially this trade off playing out in public.

Different networks have made different choices about where to sit on this trade off. Delegated proof of stake networks, covered in the previous chapter, deliberately shrink the validator set to gain speed, accepting less decentralization. Other networks try to preserve a broad, decentralized base layer and instead push additional transaction volume onto separate systems layered on top of it, an approach covered across the next several chapters on on-chain versus off-chain design, layer 1, and layer 2 solutions.

The key habit of mind this chapter aims to build is skepticism toward any scaling claim that does not say what it gave up. A blockchain that claims dramatically higher throughput than Bitcoin or Ethereum has almost certainly made a specific, identifiable trade off somewhere in decentralization or security to get there, and figuring out exactly what that trade off is, rather than just admiring the throughput number, is the right way to evaluate the claim.
